summary: Psalm 13 begins with repeated “How long” questions addressed to Yahweh, describing felt abandonment, inward sorrow, and an enemy’s triumph. The speaker then asks God to answer and preserve his life, so that enemies will not claim victory. The poem ends with trust, rejoicing, and a promise to sing because Yahweh has been good to him.
whyItMatters: This short psalm shows a common movement in Psalms from lament to petition to trust. It belongs in Book I, where many David-associated prayers voice distress while still addressing God directly.

context.author: Psalms is an anthology with many writers and collections. The heading of this psalm says, “A Psalm by David,” but Davidic headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging, and their historical origin is debated.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, later received by Jewish and Christian communities for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; assigning one date to the whole Psalter would be misleading.
context.setting: Book I of Psalms, a section dominated by David-associated prayers of distress and confidence. This poem itself names no specific event or place.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry and prayer, here a brief lament that moves through complaint, petition, trust, and praise.

outline.heading: The unanswered cry
outline.note: The speaker asks how long Yahweh will forget him and hide his face.

outline.heading: Inner sorrow and enemy pressure
outline.note: The complaint widens to daily sorrow and the enemy’s triumph.

outline.heading: A plea for life
outline.note: The speaker asks Yahweh to behold, answer, and give light to his eyes before death overtakes him.

outline.heading: Fear of enemy celebration
outline.note: The danger includes enemies claiming victory and rejoicing at his fall.

outline.heading: Trust and rejoicing
outline.note: The speaker turns to trust in loving kindness and joy in salvation.

outline.heading: A song because of goodness
outline.note: The psalm closes with a vow to sing to Yahweh because he has been good to the speaker.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David. How long, Yahweh? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the heading and opens the psalm’s main complaint: the speaker experiences God as absent or hidden.

keyVerses.text: Behold, and answer me, Yahweh, my God. Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death;
keyVerses.why: The lament becomes direct petition, asking God to answer and preserve the speaker’s life.

keyVerses.text: But I trust in your loving kindness. My heart rejoices in your salvation.
keyVerses.why: This verse marks the turn from distress to trust and joy, without narrating a changed circumstance.

keyVerses.text: I will sing to Yahweh, because he has been good to me.
keyVerses.why: The final line resolves the psalm in praise and gives the reason for the promised song.

questions.question: What is happening in this psalm?
questions.answer: The speaker feels forgotten by Yahweh, grieves every day, and is under pressure from an enemy. He asks God to answer and keep him from death, then ends by affirming trust, joy, and song. The chapter does not identify the specific crisis.

questions.question: Does “A Psalm by David” prove David wrote this exact prayer?
questions.answer: The hosted chapter’s heading says, “A Psalm by David.” Davidic headings are ancient features of the Psalter, but readers differ over whether such wording means authorship, association, dedication, or belonging. So the heading should be noticed, while the chapter itself gives no specific event from David’s life.

questions.question: Why does the psalm repeat “How long” so many times?
questions.answer: The repetition is the shape of the complaint. Verse 1 asks about being forgotten and God’s hidden face, while verse 2 asks about inner sorrow and enemy triumph. The repeated question lets the reader hear the pressure as ongoing rather than brief.

questions.question: What does “hide your face” mean here?
questions.answer: In this verse, the phrase describes the speaker’s experience of God as absent or unresponsive. The line is paired with “Will you forget me forever?” so the issue is not that God has a physical face in view, but that the speaker feels deprived of God’s attention and help. The psalm does not explain why this is happening.

questions.question: Is “soul” a separate spiritual part of the person here?
questions.answer: The verse says, “How long shall I take counsel in my soul,” and pairs it with “having sorrow in my heart every day.” In this poem, “soul” helps describe the speaker’s inward struggle and self-counsel under distress. Psalms can use compressed poetic language, so the safest reading is to describe the felt inner life without building a full theory from one word.

questions.question: What does “Give light to my eyes” ask for?
questions.answer: The next phrase says, “lest I sleep in death,” so the request is bound to survival and renewed life. The speaker asks Yahweh to behold, answer, and prevent death. Readers may hear more than one shade in the image, but the verse itself ties it to being kept from death.

questions.question: Who is the enemy?
questions.answer: The psalm does not name the enemy. It says the enemy is triumphing, may claim, “I have prevailed against him,” and that adversaries may rejoice if the speaker falls. The threat could be personal, social, legal, military, or poetic; the chapter itself leaves it unspecified.

questions.question: Does the ending mean the trouble is already gone?
questions.answer: The psalm does not report that the enemy disappeared or that circumstances changed. It shifts from petition to trust: “But I trust in your loving kindness.” The ending shows a change in the speaker’s posture before Yahweh, not a narrated rescue scene.

questions.question: How can this chapter help a first-time reader understand Psalms?
questions.answer: It shows that Psalms can speak to God with direct protest, not only praise. It also shows that a poem may move quickly: complaint in verses 1–2, petition in verses 3–4, and trust and song in verses 5–6. That movement is part of how the Psalter teaches prayer without requiring every psalm to sound calm.

glossary.def: The heading addresses this psalm to the “Chief Musician.” musical directions are preserved in Psalms, though the ancient melodies and exact force of several performance terms are lost.
The divine name used in the hosted World English Bible text of this psalm. The speaker addresses Yahweh directly in complaint, petition, and praise.
In verse 2, the speaker says he takes counsel in his “soul,” paired with sorrow in his heart. Here it names inward distress and self-deliberation within the poem.
The quality in which the speaker trusts in verse 5. In the psalm’s movement, trust in Yahweh’s loving kindness answers the earlier fear of abandonment.
What the speaker’s heart rejoices in at the turn of the psalm. In context it is tied to Yahweh’s help against death and enemy triumph.
